query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.material_initial_state: Defect-free bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloy synthesized with controlled low oxygen contamination (≈0.12 wt.% via spark plasma sintering) to represent intrinsic HEA behavior.
generation.intervention: Develop a dual-scale computational framework that independently models lattice thermal conductivity using ML-trained interatomic potentials (trained on extensive DFT datasets capturing force-constant disorder) and electronic conductivity using DFT-coupled Drude-Lorentz models. The protocol includes rigorous cross-validation with binary/ternary alloy subsystems and incorporates calibration for minor oxygen impacts.
generation.conditions: Operative over a broad temperature range from approximately 200 K up to 1200 K; samples must be fabricated to minimize extrinsic defects so that intrinsic properties dominate.
generation.structural_mediator: Intrinsic chemical disorder and atomic-scale force-constant fluctuations captured via ML force fields, coupled with independently assessed changes in plasma frequency and relaxation time for electron transport.
generation.mechanism: The approach decouples the prediction of lattice thermal conductivity – calculated from ML-trained force fields that accurately capture phonon scattering due to force-constant disorder – from electronic heat conduction, which is modeled via DFT-derived Drude-Lorentz parameters. This dual-scale method prevents conflation of underlying mechanisms, ensuring that each component is benchmarked against independent observables.
generation.predicted_outcome: Total thermal conductivity predictions within ±10–20% of experimental measurements across 200–1200 K, representing an order-of-magnitude improvement over simpler linear combination methods based solely on Debye approximations.
generation.baseline: Earlier predictive approaches that use single-parameter (e.g., Debye temperature) models or linear combinations of pure-element properties, lacking explicit decoupling between lattice and electronic transport.
generation.boundary: Applicable to defect-free or near-ideal bulk specimens. The method relies on the availability of extensive, high-quality ML training data and may require readjustment for samples with higher levels of oxygen or other impurities.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of improvement in predictive accuracy depends on the quality and transferability of the ML-trained force fields. While prior literature supports ML applications in simpler systems, uncertainties persist regarding scaling to quinary alloys; however, calibration on binary/ternary analogues and minor oxygen corrections should mitigate these risks.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate high-purity HfNbTaTiZr samples and perform temperature-dependent total thermal conductivity measurements alongside independent determination of lattice conductivity (via low-temperature modulation methods) and electronic conductivity (using terahertz spectroscopy). Compare the sum of the separately predicted values with the measured total conductivity.
measurements: Low-temperature separation of lattice and electronic contributions using modulation techniques
DFT evaluations of plasma frequency and electron relaxation times for Drude-Lorentz modeling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the combined predictions of lattice and electronic conductivity deviate from measured total conductivity by more than ±20%, or if the decoupling between the models fails (e.g., significant cross-interactions are observed), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To build a conduction model of HEAs, we start from the fundamental theory of free electrons in a conductor. According to a classical-electromagnetic theory, the frequency-dependent conductivity can be represented by the Drude-Lorentz model. The Drude model considers the conductivity contributed by the displacement of free electrons, i.e., intraband contributions. The Lorentz model takes into account the conductivity contributed by electrons bound by atomic nuclei, i.e., interband contributions. Therefore, the conductivity behavior under a low-frequency external electric field is mainly described by the Drude model, while the conductivity behavior under a high-frequency (greater than 1012 Hz) external electric field is primarily described by the Lorentz model. Calculations were conducted to compare three evaluation methods in an attempt to find a more feasible approach to predict the low-frequency conductivity of HEAs. The three compared methods are described as follows: (1) Method 1: This is the traditional linear combination method. It starts with the conductivity of pure elements and estimates the conductivity of HEAs composed of these elements by linearly combining their composi

As mentioned in the introduction, it is worth comparing the vibrational dynamics of our HEA to glasses and to crystalline materials with very large unit cells (CMAs), to identify similarities and differences and establish the place of HEAs with respect to these classes of materials. Specifically, as previously said, the low and weakly temperature dependent thermal conductivity in glasses has been associated to the existence of a strong phonon scattering due to the intrinsic disorder. Such regime, characterized by ΓFWHM ∝ (ℏω)4, has been reported in some glasses at energies corresponding to the deviation of the GVDOS from the Debye behavior and has lately been ascribed mostly to the force-constant disorder at a nanometric lengthscale. Interestingly, the same phenomenology arises in random matrix approaches, which model the vibrational properties of a glass through a random network of force-constants over a regular lattice, quite similarly to the case of our HEA,. It is thus important to check weather the same behavior can be found in our HEA, where force-constant fluctuations are the dominant phonon scattering source.
